howDoI.q: How do I draw a picture bigger than one block?
How do I make scenery Lena can walk through?
How do I use one block in many places?
How do I make a wall Lena cannot walk through?
How do I see how many blocks a game has used?

pages.head: Welcome
pages.html:
Welcome

150 Blocks is a Starter: a small game that shows a few Game-Maker ideas, with signs in the levels that say what you are looking at. It has two short levels about the 150 blocks a game gets, and takes a few minutes to finish.

Play it first. Then open it in Game-Maker (Edit a copy on the home page keeps the original safe) and read the pages below, which say where each idea is made.

The keys

Left and Right walk. Space jumps. F2 shows your lives and score. Walk into the door at the end of a level to go on.

The one idea

Every picture in a level is made of blocks, 20 by 20 pixels each, and a game has room for 150 of them. A picture bigger than one block is cut up like tiles, and a block can be used in as many places as you like. So the way to draw a lot is to draw a little, and use it again.

pages.head: Level 1: One Big Picture
pages.html:
Level 1: One Big Picture

Three signs stand before a stone tower. ONE BIG PICTURE IS MANY BLOCKS says what it is. THIS TOWER TOOK 18 BLOCKS counts them: it is four blocks wide and five high, which is twenty places, but the empty corners are plain sky and use the sky block that was already there. A PICTURE IS NOT SOLID. WALK IN asks Lena to try it, and they walk right in through the door and out the other side.

Four coins lie past the tower, and two more are up in the air. Jump for those.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 1 is made

  • Cut into tiles. Open blocks.bbl in the blocks editor and find the blocks named tower. The tower was drawn once as one picture, 80 by 100 pixels, then cut into twenty 20 by 20 squares. Each square is a block, and the editor shows them in order.
  • Laid in the map. Open one.map in the map editor and find the tower: its blocks are set in a rectangle, four across and five down, in the same order they were cut. Put them anywhere in that shape and the picture comes back together.
  • Empty corners cost nothing. The four squares at the top corners are only sky, so the map uses the plain sky block there. No new block was needed.
  • Not solid. Every tower block has Gravity down and no Solid sides, like sky, so Lena walks through and falls through. A picture is only a wall if you check Solid on its blocks.
  • The count. The sign beside it is a picture too, made of its own blocks. Signs spend blocks as well, so a game with many signs has fewer left for art.

pages.head: Level 2: Use It Again
pages.html:
Level 2: Use It Again

The ONE BLOCK CAN BE USED AGAIN sign comes first, then 8 HOUSES, ONLY 6 BLOCKS. Eight little houses stand in a row, red roofs and blue roofs taking turns, and they are made from six blocks between them. Past them, EVERY COPY ACTS THE SAME stands before a brick wall. Lena walks into it and stops, then jumps over.

The last sign counts every block in the game against the 150. Nine coins in all, some of them above the houses and above the sign.

pages.head: How this level is made
pages.html:
How level 2 is made

  • Six blocks, thirty-two places. A house is two blocks wide and two high, and each has a roof on top and a wall with a window and a door below. The red and the blue house have different roofs but the same walls, so the walls are the same two blocks in both. That makes six blocks: four roof pieces and two wall pieces. Open two.map and see the same names again and again.
  • Used again. A block costs one of the 150 however many times the map uses it. A thousand copies and one copy cost the same. What takes room is a picture that is different in every place.
  • Every copy acts the same. The rules of a block (solid, gravity, points) belong to the block, not to the place it is put. The brick wall is the brick block, so every brick of it is solid. A look-alike that Lena could walk through would need to be a block of its own, with its own rules.
  • The count. Count the blocks in blocks.bbl. The last sign says how many there are.

pages.head: What it cannot do
pages.html:
What it cannot do

These are the engine’s limits, so you can plan around them.

  • More than 150 blocks. The background set has 150 places and no more. The editor stops you at the end, and a game cannot swap blocks in and out while it runs.
  • A block cannot be flipped or turned. A mirror image of a block is a second block, drawn by hand. A symmetric picture still needs both halves, unless its halves are the same.
  • A block cannot act differently in two places. Solid, gravity, points and what it turns into all belong to the block. A tree that is solid at the trunk and not at the leaves needs different blocks.
  • A picture cannot be larger than the map. A big picture is only ever a group of blocks, and the game has no idea they belong together. Nothing moves them as one.
  • Blocks are 20 by 20 pixels. There is no other size and no scaling.

pages.head: Make it yours
pages.html:
Make it yours

Try one change at a time, and play after each:

  • In one.map, swap two of the tower’s blocks and see the picture break.
  • Check Solid on one tower block and walk into it.
  • Draw a third house color in blocks.bbl by changing only a roof, and see how few blocks it takes.
  • Remove the brick wall by painting sky over it, or build a taller one.
  • Count the blocks in blocks.bbl before and after you add a sign.

The home page’s Starters tab has more small games like this one.

box.back: A small explorer in a red beanie walks through a tower that is only a picture, then past a row of eight houses made from six blocks. A game gets 150 blocks, and a clever one makes them go a long way. Read the signs, then open the game in Game-Maker and see how many blocks it spent.
features: Signs in the levels explain each idea
A big picture is a group of blocks, and a block can be used again
Made to be copied and taken apart

blurb: Two short levels about the 150 blocks a game gets. A picture bigger than one block is a group of blocks, cut like tiles, and a block used again costs nothing more. A stone tower is one picture that Lena walks right through, and a row of houses is built from a few blocks used again and again. Signs in the levels say how, and the last one counts the game's blocks. Play it, then open it in Game-Maker and look at the Blocks tab.
